analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal construction contractors to pay local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act was referred to committee and never received a vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, on the books since 1931, requires companies doing federally financed construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage. This bill would wipe that requirement out, letting contractors pay whatever wages they choose on federal projects. It was introduced by Rep. Bob Inglis with four Republican cosponsors and never advanced beyond a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Contractors on federally financed construction projects, who could cut labor costs by paying less than the local prevailing wage. Contractors bidding against each other could lower bids by reducing wages, and firms that pay low wages would find it easier to win federal work.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act outright, ending the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction be paid locally prevailing wages [S2][S3].
Makes the repeal effective five days after enactment, while leaving existing contracts untouched [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, who could see their pay drop where prevailing-wage rules were the only thing holding it at the local standard, including overtime and hours protections tied to the Act.

drawbacks.text: The Davis-Bacon Act exists to prevent contractors from cutting workers' pay below the local standard and from importing lower-wage crews into federal projects; repeal removes that floor [S2].
Supporters of the Act have long argued it protects local contractors and workers from being undercut by outside low-bid firms; repeal would shift bargaining power to employers on federal jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear cost saving to federal construction contractors, but the cost falls on the workers whose wages the Act protects. Whether repeal would also save taxpayers money depends entirely on contractors passing lower labor costs through to the government rather than keeping them, and the bill contains no mechanism guaranteeing that.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the 103rd Congress ended with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Inglis introduced the bill on February 2, 1994, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
On February 11, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where it stayed for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal construction workers and the local-wage standards that protect them are better off, since the repeal never advanced; contractors who wanted to pay less than prevailing wage on federal projects did not get that change.

for.name: Rep. Bob Inglis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Abolition Act to repeal the prevailing wage law.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee / Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and never scheduled it for consideration or a vote.

against.name: Organized labor and prevailing-wage advocates
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of Davis-Bacon repeal, defending the prevailing wage standard on federal construction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote to show broader support or opposition.

industries.note: Repeal would free contractors on federally financed projects from paying the local prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs. Workers' pay would bear that saving, and there is no guarantee it reaches taxpayers.

industries.industry: Construction labor unions and unionized building-trades workers
industries.note: The prevailing wage standard has been a core protection for union-scale pay on federal projects; repeal would remove the floor that keeps federal work at local standards and undercuts union contractors.
